 By Neelanjit Das , ET Online Last Updated: Nov 16, 2026, 02:57:16 PM IST Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment Synopsis
 A.Masilamani was faced with eviction from government land that he inherited from his mother due to the Grama Natham rules. The court clarified that if the conditions of the grant are violated, the inheritance loses validity. Legal heirs are only eligible for government land if they meet the qualifications set after the original assignee’s death. Listen to this article in summarized format
 Listen ET Online Authorities started eviction proceedings against son from his late mother’s land after he sought patta transfer; authorities cited violation of conditional patta terms; son files case but loses in Madras HC A recent Madras High Court judgement shows how individuals who have got free land from the government as grant should follow all the terms and conditions attached to this grant, else their children can lose this land. This is the story of A.Masilamani whose mother was given 3 cents of land under the Grama Natham rules regulated by the Tamil Nadu Government.
 Grama Natham land is owned by the Tamil Nadu government and are given to landless poor people for housing public use. However, certain specific conditions are attached to these lands, which if violated, allows the government to take back the land . This is the ground on which the government wanted to evict A.Masilamani saying that his mother had violated the terms and conditions of the Grama Natham lands.
A. Masilamani challenged the eviction in court. He argued that the government had no right to evict him as he had inherited this land from his mother, even though it was Grama Natham land. 
On November 4, 2026, the Madras High Court ruled that no inheritance of Grama Natham land is possible if the terms and conditions of the grant are violated. The government could therefore reclaim the land and A. Masilamani had to vacate it. But the court made it clear that A. Masilamani could pursue other legal remedies if he wished.

 Why did the son lose the case?
Asha Kiran Sharma, Partner at King Stubb and Kasiva, said to ET Wealth Online : Masilamani lost on three counts. The first reason is Masilamani did not file the statutory appeal under Section 10 of the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905.
According to Sharma, the second reason why Masilamani (son) lost the case is because he incorrectly argued that Grama Natham land does not vest in the Government and so the Tahsildar cannot invoke the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905.
Sharma says that the third reason why he lost the case is because the Madras High Court held that land assigned on conditions cannot turn into hereditary property. Under Revenue Standing Orders 21 and 26, Grama Natham land is assigned to landless poor persons, up to a limited extent, on conditions. When the assignee dies, officials must check whether the heirs are eligible. If they are not, the land can go to another eligible poor person.
 Madras High Court discussion
The Madras High Court observed that the primary contention of A. Masilamani was that the g overnment land was granted to his mother and after her demise, he as a legal heir, submitted an application for change of patta. However, his application was rejected and the authorities instead sought his eviction.
The Madras High Court said that if the legal heirs of the original assignee (which is the mother in this case) are found to be ineligible, such legal heirs (son in this case) would not be entitled to get a transfer of Patta.
The Madras High Court ruled that a conditional assignment of g overnment land cannot be passed on through succession as hereditary property. The land remains g overnment property and its assignment is subject to terms and conditions stipulated under the Revenue Standing Orders.
After the death of the original assignee, the authorities may investigate whether the legal heirs qualify to receive Government land free of charge. ,If they do not qualify, the land may be assigned to another eligible poor person by following the procedures set out under the Revenue Standing Orders. In the present case, the assignee (the mother) had violated the conditions.
The Madras High Court said that in the case of S.Anbananthan, it was decided by a division bench of the court that Grama Natham lands may be occupied only under the authority of law and mere occupation of Grama Natham lands would not confer any ownership to an individual.
The Madras High Court said that the R evenue Standing Orders would have the force of law and further contemplated that the occupants of Grama Natham lands without authority of law would be treated as encroachers and the Government would be empowered to evict those encroachers by following the procedures under the provisions of the Act, 1905.
The Madras High Court said that A.Masilamani has not preferred any statutory appeal as contemplated under Section 10 of the Act, 1905.
The Madras High Court said: “Exhausting the efficacious alternate remedy contemplated under the Act 1905 is of paramount importance. The original authority, namely, Tahsildar relied on the revenue documents and, considering the violations against conditional patta, not considered the case of the petitioner for grant of transfer of patta. Thus, the challenges made against the notices are not entertainable.” (Join our ETWealth WhatsApp channel for all the latest updates)
